title: Netflix Bets ‘Ink’ and Its Timely Rupert Murdoch Story Can Win Oscars for Danny Boyle and Guy Pearce
description:
Netflix wants the “ink” to dry on its Oscar prospects.

	Danny Boyle made his first trip to Venice with “Ink,” his adaptation of James Graham’s stag
body:
Netflix wants the “ink” to dry on its Oscar prospects.

	Danny Boyle made his first trip to Venice with “Ink,” his adaptation of James Graham’s stage sensation, which opened the 83rd edition in competition before moving through Telluride and Toronto, with the streamer giving it a December theatrical release and a January streaming date.

	The early temperature is reading warm. “Ink” drew a four-minute standing ovation on opening night in Venice, and the reactions filtering out of Telluride have been buzzing across the mountains, the kind of enthusiasm and respect a Netflix campaign is built to amplify.
	

	The subject is an origin myth of modern media: Rupert Murdoch’s 1969 acquisition of a dying tabloid called The Sun and the rapid transformation that followed. Graham, adapting his own Tony-nominated play, approaches the story with the mechanics of a heist. Boyle supplies the velocity.


	The central question is not simply how Murdoch built a newspaper. It is how two men helped invent the modern attention economy that shapes all of our lives today.

	Guy Pearce plays a brash, thirty-something Murdoch, an outsider with a chip on his shoulder and a plan for disrupting Fleet Street. Jack O’Connell plays editor Larry Lamb, the working-class newspaperman Murdoch pushes past every line the establishment believes cannot be crossed.

	Both actors have obvious awards narratives, but two very different categories to break into.

	Pearce arrives two years after his first Oscar nomination, a supporting actor bid for “The Brutalist,” which gives him the benefit of recent Academy recognition. And the role could hardly be more of the moment. Murdoch is a figure many hold responsible for the fractured, combustible information environment the U.S. is living through right now and there is a particular charge in watching an actor humanize the young man who lit the fuse. That timeliness is the kind of thing that fuels an Oscar campaign.
	

	O’Connell arrives with something different: momentum. Between “Sinners” and the “28 Years Later” films, he is coming off a stretch that has significantly raised his visibility. Being a hot commodity right now, and perhaps even a package deal with Pearce in voters’ minds, could give him a fighting shot in a very crowded best actor field.

	We have seen roles like Pearce’s cakewalk to nominations before, purely on the nature of the part, even when pundits wrote them off early. Look at the run of real-life figures who landed supporting bids: Jon Voight in “Ali” (2001), Matt Damon in “Invictus” (2009), Kenneth Branagh in “My Week with Marilyn” (2011), Christopher Plummer in “All the Money in the World” (2017), Sam Rockwell in “Vice” (2018), J.K. Simmons in “Being the Ricardos” (2021) and Jeremy Strong in “The Apprentice” (2024).

	Pearce may not have the most screen time, but he is memorable in every frame. O’Connell has the more obvious breakout narrative and, as the story’s beating heart, the showier dramatic arc.

	Two performances from one film can coexist comfortably in an awards campaign, but they can also create a strategic problem. The distributor must establish why both actors are essential without letting voters perceive one as stealing oxygen from the other.



	

					Guy Pearce as Rupert Murdoch and Jack O’Connell as Larry Lamb in “Ink”
									Netflix
	



	There is also a screenplay story here, and a recent precedent worth studying.

	Graham is adapting his own acclaimed play, which puts “Ink” in the adapted screenplay conversation and on a path that “One Night in Miami” walked in 2020. That film, too, launched at Venice and Kemp Powers turned his own stage work into an adapted screenplay nomination while the movie also landed an acting nod for Leslie Odom Jr. A playwright translating his own material, a festival launch and a performance the industry embraces: the template is right there.

	But Netflix will look to check even more boxes.

	Beyond the two actors, “Ink” is built to contend in the crafts. Its production design, by Carson McColl and Gareth Pugh, rebuilds a vanished Fleet Street. Fin Oates cuts the film with a fragmented, kinetic energy that recalls the associative style Hank Corwin brought to Adam McKay’s “The Big Short” and “Vice.” Johnnie Burn, the Oscar-winning sound designer of “The Zone of Interest,” lends the film one of the most decorated ears in the business. And composer Daniel Pemberton supplies an original score with the propulsion Boyle’s movies demand, capping a bombastic year that also includes “Project Hail Mary.”
	

	Netflix has the resources to make all of those cases.

	The larger question is whether the company has the bandwidth. Its fall slate is stacked, with “La Bola Negra,” “The Adventures of Cliff Booth,” “Possible Love,” “Gentle Monster” and “The Mosquito Bowl” all angling for the same oxygen. “Ink” will have to compete not only against rival distributors but against Netflix’s own contenders for screeners, headlines, events, Q & As and voter attention. The Venice-Telluride-Toronto sequence helps enormously, giving the movie the sort of early critical footprint that can turn an awards campaign into a sustained conversation.

	And Boyle’s presence adds another narrative. As the Oscar-winning filmmaker behind “Slumdog Millionaire,” he brings such a distinctive visual and kinetic signature that the fall circuit was an obvious place for the film to bow.

	The James Graham connection gives “Ink” a larger cultural context. His work has repeatedly mined the intersection of power, institutions and public life, from politics to journalism. “Ink” arrives in a media environment in which the questions surrounding Murdoch’s influence feel less like history than an origin story for the world audiences inhabit now.

	That resonance is the film’s best weapon, and the campaign will not have to manufacture it.

	“Ink” argues that we are all still living in the paper they printed.

schema.headline: Netflix Bets ‘Ink’ and Its Timely Rupert Murdoch Story Can Win Oscars for Danny Boyle and Guy Pearce

title: John Turturro Has Waited 40 Years for an Oscar Nomination. ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Makes the Case
description: Forty years into a career that has made him one of American cinema’s most recognizable character actors, John Turturro has a Cannes best actor prize
body:
Forty years into a career that has made him one of American cinema’s most recognizable character actors, John Turturro has a Cannes best actor prize, an enviable résumé and exactly zero Oscar mornings when his name was read aloud with the words “and the nominees are.”

	Sony Pictures Classics is determined to end the drought with his work in the acclaimed “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” which premiered at Sundance last January and made its fall festival bow at Telluride this weekend, where the film and Turturro’s invigorating turn as an aging pickpocket are drawing acclaim.
	

	Turturro, 69, has been making the rounds in the Colorado mountains, attending Q&As and a Saturday night dinner hosted by Sony Pictures Classics, where writer-director Noah Segan mingled with press and industry attendees.


	Turturro has spent four decades operating in the space reserved for actors everyone recognizes and almost nobody thinks of as an Oscar nominee. He has worked with masters of cinema such as the Coen brothers, Spike Lee and Robert Redford and has appeared opposite everyone from Tom Hanks to Adam Sandler. He’s played gangsters, professors, detectives, eccentrics, husbands, fathers and men who seem to have wandered into the wrong movie and somehow made it better.

	And yet, the Academy has never invited him to the party.

	And it’s not like he hasn’t been close. Turturro won best actor at Cannes for the Coen brothers’ “Barton Fink” in 1991. Three years later, his combustible Herbie Stempel in Robert Redford’s “Quiz Show” collected Golden Globe and SAG Award nominations, the kind of precursor support that usually precedes an Oscar bid. But each time, the industry seemed to look elsewhere.
	

	The television world has been kinder. His weary defense attorney in “The Night Of,” HBO’s 2016 crime drama, drew Emmy, Golden Globe and SAG Award nominations. His tender, unraveling Irving Bailiff on “Severance,” Apple TV’s dystopian workplace thriller, has since earned him two Emmy nominations, the most recent lost to his own castmate Tramell Tillman in 2025.

	“The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” can change that.



	

	



	In a similar vein to Richard Jenkins’ first career nomination for the 2007 drama “The Visitor,” Turturro can be the overdue veteran to finally see his name in lights. Segan’s Sundance breakout, acquired by SPC for a fall release, gives Turturro something four decades of great supporting performances never could: a movie that he leads, one that lives and dies on him.

	He plays Harry Lehman, an analog thief operating in a city where the very concept of pickpocketing has become obsolete. Wallets increasingly contain less cash, phones have replaced maps and tickets and two-factor authentication has made the modern world almost aggressively hostile to the old-fashioned criminal. Harry is clinging to a disappearing profession while caring for his ailing wife, Rosie.

	While that metaphor is hardly subtle, it’s also part of its appeal. Harry is not simply a thief whose trade is dying; he’s a man confronting his own obsolescence.

	SPC calls it the finest performance of Turturro’s career. Distributor hyperbole is usually best treated as campaign copy. But here, it resonates. Turturro has never been an actor who needed to announce himself. He slips into other people’s scenes, finds the detail nobody else thought to play and then, almost imperceptibly, becomes the most interesting person in the room. The Academy has rewarded that instinct repeatedly, just not when Turturro has been the person standing at the center of the frame.

	As an awards campaign, the studio is following a familiar formula: a beloved, never-nominated veteran finally gets a leading role worthy of his gifts. But the strongest version of the pitch is not “Give John Turturro an Oscar.” It is “Look at what John Turturro has been doing all along.”

	The Academy has historically responded to overdue narratives, particularly when the performance provides a credible reason to act on the sentiment. Turturro has the résumé, the festival pedigree and the late-career showcase that can turn years of admiration into a voting impulse.
	

	“The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” is a movie about a man whose skills belong to another era, trying to prove they still have value. The meta-text is impossible to miss. Turturro’s awards case makes essentially the same argument about the actor himself.

	It also helps to have Steve Buscemi in the cast, who could mount his own first awards run for “Wild Horse Nine,” along with the best awards campaigner this side of the sun, Jamie Lee Curtis, who delivers a killer one-scene wonder.

	Like a lot of SPC films, neither the movie nor Turturro may seem the loudest voice in the room right now and plenty of pundits will write it off early, especially once precursors start rolling in. But as the studio has shown with titles like “The Father,” “Parallel Mothers” and “I’m Still Here,” the ground game and striking when it matters most, is what wins these campaigns.

	And Turturro may not even be the film’s only awards story. Segan, long a familiar face in front of the camera, wrote and directed “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” himself and a spare, mournful original like this one is exactly the kind of writer-director calling card the original screenplay race tends to reward. It happens more than voters remember. “Frozen River,” another SPC sleeper, paired Melissa Leo’s lead nomination with a surprise original screenplay nod for writer-director Courtney Hunt and “Nebraska” did the same for Bruce Dern and scribe Bob Nelson. If the film connects with voters, Segan’s script could ride in alongside its star.

	The best actor field, notably, is shaping up to be incredibly crowded. Heading into the fall festivals, pundits had already penciled in the likes of Matt Damon (“The Odyssey”), Ryan Gosling (“Project Hail Mary”) and Sebastian Stan (“Fjord”), and Venice and Telluride added John Malkovich (“Wild Horse Nine”) and Andrew Scott (“Elsinore”) to the conversation. SPC will have to make noise without overselling a performance whose appeal lies in its subtlety. But if the campaign can persuade voters to see Harry not as a novelty but as the culmination of everything Turturro has spent a career doing, the narrative becomes difficult to ignore.

	Let’s see if this pickpocket can steal some hearts along the way.

schema.headline: John Turturro Has Waited 40 Years for an Oscar Nomination. ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Makes the Case

title: ‘Woman Unknown’ Review: Some More Problematic Sex — and Its Consequences — by Denmark’s May el-Toukhy
description: Against the rubble gray and stiff mahogany with which director May el-Toukhy washes out her post-Second World War Copenhagen, the pops of crimson in
body:
Against the rubble gray and stiff mahogany with which director May el-Toukhy washes out her post-Second World War Copenhagen, the pops of crimson in “Woman Unknown” announce a stark symbolism that’s about as subtle as the red swastika eventually smeared on the front door of protagonist Marie (Mathilde Arcel). As obvious as these subliminal scarlet letters may be, they’re not without a certain Hitchcockian power in a film about sexual shame and a kind of violence against women’s bodies that operates from the inside out. But as this is el-Toukhy — whose steely 2019 incest drama “Queen of Hearts” was promptly adapted by French provocatrice Catherine Breillat in “Last Summer” — the film’s feminism, or lack thereof depending on how you take your empowerment, is a prickly matter by design. 
	

	As with the women played by Emmanuelle Riva in “Hiroshima, Mon Amour” or Charlotte Rampling in “The Night Porter,” a crisis is sparked over Marie’s supposedly soiled sheets, with el-Toukhy basing her story on the many accounts of public punishment received by women from Nazi-occupied countries who had sexual relations with German soldiers during the war. It’s a spicy conceit from the only woman director in Venice’s main competition, and its implications arguably creep out beyond the historical context in question — should our private lives be judged and exposed to real consequences? Not that el-Toukhy has made a particularly open film with this neatly scripted psychodrama, her austere visuals and prim haut-bourgeois setting practically asking to be unraveled. 
	

	Marie, a maid and nanny to the twiggy blonde child of her employer Christian (Carsten Bjornlund), a widower and owner of a glove-making factory, carries herself as if permanently bound in a corset: breath held, mouth tight, her eyes shifty as if dreading the next reprimand. It makes sense given her workplace’s exacting standards, in which place settings are arranged according to centimeter-precise measurements and stony head maid Esther (Marina Bouras) is always watching. 

	But early on, when Christian discreetly caresses Marie’s cheek, it’s clear that it’s not just her job that’s at stake should she fall, but her newly gained status as lady of the house. A long shot of a pearly silk dress — a wedding dress — dangling like a carrot in an empty closet doubles as a harbinger of doom when she’s spotted by Karl (Thorbjorn Hedegaard), an old classmate from her hometown who’s much too eager to catch up. It’s through this jittery encounter, and a visit to the doctor where Marie re-ups on the liquid opium she takes to dull the pain of sex with Christian, that we learn she once had a baby boy, and that child caused her to flee her past life. 

	El-Toukhy and Maren Louise Kaehne’s script doesn’t connect the dots for you with explanatory dialogue, but those dots are still awfully close. Scenes of nameless women being knocked around on the streets by gangs of men, who chop off their hair and tear off their clothes before branding them with painted swastikas, make it brutally clear what Marie is hiding from. And what starts out with the echoing, empty rooms of paranoia turns into whispers from the domestic staff after Karl discovers where Marie lives. The building door is marked with Nazi insignia shortly after, leaving Marie desperate to cover the tracks that lead to her. 

	Cinematographer Jasper Spanning’s static, shadowy frames give way to shallow-lensed close-ups as Marie plunges into a panicked spiral that, at one point, sees her consenting to a wad of spit in her mouth. That scene, which begins with a pan over Marie’s naked body as Karl swats her hands away to do as he pleases, rhymes with comparably frigid moments involving the gilded milieu she aspires to join — as when a snooty tailor takes her measurements or when Christian uses her as a hand model to show off a new glove design. This body does not belong to her, and her refusal to cede control of it to her male masters will end in their wrath, a point made repeatedly, albeit with a harrowing range of registers. 
	

	Marie’s humanity and capacity for tenderness come through in her scenes with children, though these aren’t nearly weighty enough — despite Arcel’s commendably nervy performance —  to carry out her concluding crash-out convincingly. Her relationship with the next-door neighbor, a single mother far too liberated to escape scrutiny in midcentury Denmark, gets a few threadbare scenes to prime this spiritual flurry, where red appears one last time in the form of blood on Marie’s hands. Worse than the loogie is the feminine betrayal that weighs on her soul, or at least that’s how it’s supposed to read.

schema.headline: ‘Woman Unknown’ Review: Some More Problematic Sex — and Its Consequences — by Denmark’s May el-Toukhy

title: ‘The Echo Chamber’ Review: Luca Marinelli, Alicia Vikander and Susan Sarandon Reverberate Through a Smoky, Somber Single-Location Love Story
description: If you’re ever thinking of attempting a single-location film, choose that location with care. Make it high-ceilinged, light-filled, book-lined, with
body:
If you’re ever thinking of attempting a single-location film, choose that location with care. Make it high-ceilinged, light-filled, book-lined, with a reading-nook conservatory area, a gargantuan sofa, a killer sound system and space enough that you don’t even have to turn sideways to sidle past the grand piano. If possible, have it overlook a neatly cobbled, colonnaded street where one can park one’s classic car. In short, make it the luscious London flat in which all of Andrea Pallaoro‘s “The Echo Chamber” takes place. When Anne (Alicia Vikander), a doctor who does house calls, tells her patient Leonardo (Luca Marinelli), a music producer suffering from chronic lower back pain, “I really like your apartment. There’s so many interesting things to look at,” it signals the beginning of a tentatively passionate love story, that perhaps only a man as secure as Leonardo — who looks like Luca Marinelli — could be certain is directed at him, and not his highly desirable residence.
	

	Of course, the idea that where you live is actually an extension of who you are — especially if one lives the kind of successful, worldly, creatively fulfilled life that Leo apparently does — is very central here. Based on the screenplay that Bernardo Bertolucci was writing with collaborators Ilaria Bernardini and Ludovica Rampoldi at the time of his death in 2018, “The Echo Chamber’s” constraints actually come less from its single-location conceit than from its own limited interest in expanding on the inner worlds of its protagonists, beyond their endless involvement in their own fraught relationship. Not to say we’re not to some extent involved too: It is always nice to watch attractive people fall in love, and then run into the kind of obstacles that allow them to pine for each other in the most attractive of ways.
	

	The film is certainly beautiful, shot in gorgeously rich Academy-ratio frames by Apichatpong, Reygadas and Refn collaborator Diego Garcia, who makes portraiture and still life out of every single closeup, and landscapes out of the different planes that can be achieved through the modular lighting and glass panels of Gaspare de Pascali’s exquisite production design. And, at least until a highly unnecessary eleventh-hour swerve into melodrama, it is directed with great sensitivity and restraint by Pallaoro, who has never once been guilty of overstatement across his three fine previous features: “Medeas,” “Monica” and “Hannah.” 

	But despite an enlivening turn from Susan Sarandon, playing a singing icon whom Leo has tempted out of semi-retirement to record an album of new songs, and despite Vikander and Marinelli playing off each other nicely, it does not fire the imagination beyond the confines of these four walls. (Actually maybe 10 or 12, given the workspace, bedroom, bathroom, etc.) Long before the end of its overstretched two-hours-plus, and certainly well before that overwrought final-act twist, it feels like we have put in rather too much time with this couple, and maybe we ought to just leave them to it.

	Told in a flashback-and-forward structure, the film starts in the middle of the timeline, at the point of the relationship’s biggest crisis. Anne comes back to the apartment (the pair do not live together, though she has a key) to discover Leo, high on pain meds, sporting a wrist cast, leaping around the living room to deafening, noise-ordinance-defying music. Initially concerned, she cannot help but be infected by his contagious, if chemically-induced, good humor and they party for a bit. But later, she wakes up on top of him on the sofa and he will not wake up at all. She calls an ambulance.

	Some months later he returns, presumably from a stint in rehab, and resumes his work with Ava May (Sarandon) — an album of spooky, smoky, twilight torch ballads, written by composer/lyricist team Clément Ducol and Émilie Gassin, and well-suited to the slight husk of Sarandon’s voice. But, associating Anne with his addiction — since she was the one who first, reluctantly, gave him opioids when his debilitating back pain proved resistant to any other treatment — and on the advice of his sponsor, he puts off contacting her. Anne takes to hovering nearby and letting herself into the apartment whenever he leaves. (It is never exactly clear how she comes to be sufficiently close by to be at the kitchen window in time to watch his car pull away.)
	

	Inside she wanders around, initially furtively checking that Leo is not falling off the wagon, rummaging through cupboards, surreptitiously licking the edge of the credit card he used to cut his lines. But soon her visits have more emotional than practical purpose as, lovesick, she takes to sleeping in his bed, washing in his shower, and occasionally curling up on an armchair with one of his books. Usually, she is careful to cover her tracks, blow-drying the towel so its dampness does not give her away, plumping the sofa pillows back up just so. But at some point frustration begins to set in, and she begins to leave deliberate markers of her presence. 

	While it’s definitely true that what is romantic under certain circumstances can look at a lot stalking in others, “The Echo Chamber” is not the kind of film to probe such worldly distinctions. Leo remains unaware of Anne’s visits until she reveals them, at which point he responds in kind. And as love gestures go, getting a reclusive famous singer to re-record an early track of hers that Anne’s mother used to sing to her as child, is a pretty grand one, and when she lets herself in that day and realizes he has left it playing for her, Anne interprets it accordingly.

	It’s almost a pity, as the idea of the apartment as the go-between — holding onto and nourishing the love between two people who cannot actually be together — is undeniably poetic, and we could have spent a little more time exploring it, and a little less on the rather repetitive sneaking-around phase. And indeed, we could have used a little more Ava May, given that it’s her muse-like friendship with Leo that is the more unusual, and in some ways more touching, love story here. Ava May’s words of wisdom, about love and regret and a life apparently thoroughly hard-lived, make her the most inherently interesting character of the three, and also the most enjoyably catty. “You’re right, that Anne of yours really is an angel,” she tells Leo at one point, stubbing out her cigarette on the windowsill. “Of course, I don’t know that I really like angels.”

schema.headline: ‘The Echo Chamber’ Review: Luca Marinelli, Alicia Vikander and Susan Sarandon Reverberate Through a Smoky, Somber Single-Location Love Story

title: ‘Possible Love’ Cast Sobs as Lee Chang-dong’s Epic Embraced at Venice With 6-Minute Standing Ovation
description: Acclaimed South Korean director Lee Chang-dong returned after 24 years to the Venice Film Festival, where he was warmly embraced with a six-minute s
body:
Acclaimed South Korean director Lee Chang-dong returned after 24 years to the Venice Film Festival, where he was warmly embraced with a six-minute standing ovation for his sweeping romantic drama “Possible Love.”

	Directed by Lee and co-written by Oh Jung-mi, “Possible Love” follows the intertwined lives of two married couples — a laid-off factory worker and his spouse, and a wealthy husband and wife who are making a documentary about the injustices facing factory workers — whose lives intersect after a funeral. A meditation on social class and desire, the movie brings together familiar faces from the director’s prior work, including Jeon Do-yeon (“Secret Sunshine”) and Sul Kyung-gu (“Peppermint Candy”), as well as new collaborators in Zo In-sung (“Escape From Mogadishu”) and Cho Yeo-jeong (of “Parasite” fame). 
	

	As the credits rolled and the lights came up in the Sala Grande theater, the cast started to sob and wiped away tears with napkins. Jeon, Sul, Zo and Cho took turns hugging each other, enthusiastically clapping and giggling at their emotional response to the audience’s enthusiasm for the film. Oh, too, was crying as she basked in the rapturous applause. The claps and cheers would have possibly continued a lot longer, but at the six-minute mark, the actors and director were guided toward the exit and headed out of the Palazzo del Cinema. A major theme of “Possible Love” is the 10th commandment, “thou shalt not covet,” so perhaps the cast and filmmakers were satisfied by the reaction and didn’t need a lengthier standing ovation.
	

	“Possible Love” marks Lee’s first time in competition at Venice in nearly a quarter-century, following his Silver Lion win for “Oasis” in 2002. This is the director’s first feature film in eight years, since 2018’s psychological thriller “Burning.” His other major works include “Green Fish,” “Peppermint Candy,” “Secret Sunshine” and “Poetry.”

	“I’m not the type of filmmaker who can make movies easily,” Lee said previously of the lengthy gap between projects. “Before I begin a film, I must be certain of what it means — to me, to the audience, and to cinema itself. That is why ‘Possible Love’ took so long to make.”  

	Netflix is releasing “Possible Love,” which is making stops at Toronto and New York film festivals ahead of its theatrical rollout. The movie opens on the big screen in the U.S. on Oct. 23 before streaming globally on Nov. 6. Netflix opened this year’s Venice Film Festival with director Danny Boyle’s “Ink,” an explosive drama about the rise of Rupert Murdoch’s tabloid empire. 

	Prior to the premiere of “Possible Love,” Lee mused on the film’s title, saying “it asks a question: what is love that is possible?”

	“When we think about a love story, usually the most typical love story we think about is love that cannot come true,” Lee told Variety. “So to simply put it, you could say that all of these love stories are called impossible love.”

schema.headline: ‘Possible Love’ Cast Sobs as Lee Chang-dong’s Epic Embraced at Venice With 6-Minute Standing Ovation

title: ‘Agata the Writer’ Review: Mia Wasikowska Plays an Author Adrift and Short of Ideas, in a Sly, Witty Film With Plenty
description: As anyone who has made a great-author biopic (or even watched one, for that matter) can tell you, writing is among the hardest professions to make c
body:
As anyone who has made a great-author biopic (or even watched one, for that matter) can tell you, writing is among the hardest professions to make cinematic. The slow churn of ideas, the second-guessing and self-editing, and even those rare, exhilarating surges of creative flow are all part of a stubbornly interior, usually static process. Small wonder, then, that writer’s block is an eternally popular subject for doubtless empathetic, readily self-distracting screenwriters: Dramatic possibilities open up considerably when a character is doing something, anything, other than what they’re supposed to be doing. Yet in “Agata the Writer” — an elegant, slippery slip of a film about writing, yes, but also about immigrant identity, trauma tourism, vulgar art, theft of property and history, and strange, dissonant homecomings away from home — those possibilities also wind up perversely misbehaving.
	

	A debut of impressive poise and confidently willful storytelling instincts from video artist Kuba Dorabialski, “Agata the Writer” also marks a welcome return to substantial film roles for the ever-interesting, ever-quizzical Australian actress Mia Wasikowska — who, the last time we saw her in something of this approximate register, was a malleable figment of a writer’s imagination in Mia Hansen-Løve’s similarly meta but far breezier “Bergman Island.” As reference points go, however, this year’s gorgeous Canadian Oscar submission “Nina Roza” feels more tonally and thematically complementary.


	Future distributors may well reach for comparisons when trying to sell this pleasingly ornery, elusive film, which will likely divide viewers with its intractable narrative swerves and culs-de-sac. But it’s among the most bracingly singular works at this year’s Venice Film Festival, where it premieres in the Giornate degli Autori (formerly known in English as Venice Days) sidebar.
	

	The arch introductory narration, over the first of two bookending shots of a winding hillside road, will immediately clue viewers into the tone of things to come, as it drily, somewhat omnisciently articulates the mindset of Agata (Wasikowska), a Polish-Australian writer who has had some success with her satirical novels, but is pursuing a more earnest shift in creative direction. Inspired to write a story of a father-daughter relationship during the Bosnian War, she travels to Sarajevo, where she plans to stay a few months and research the project — hoping to find, in the narrator’s words, “a Slavic similitude” between her Polish roots and this otherwise unfamiliar locale.

	But from the moment Agata arrives in the city, she feels conspicuously out of place. Sarajevo — nothing if not a city of contrasts, to borrow a school-report cliché — presents here as wintry and severe, not unwelcoming but not overly accommodating either, painted in damp mineral shades, with a running chorus of wind, varying in volume and intensity, but seemingly never dropping entirely. Early on, we glimpse a sound recordist (Dorabialski himself) trying to capture that natural white noise on a deserted roadside; we’ll learn his story, so to speak, far later on. 

	For writers of a certain melancholy persuasion, this could be an ideal environment for some productive literary brooding. But for Agata, the more she explores Sarajevo, the less she she feels she knows it. She certainly doesn’t feel confident in her ability to set a story in its most painful period of history, despite the eager encouragement of her friend and editor Davina (Mia Morrissey), and the assistance of new acquaintance Jasmina (a superb Vedrana Božinović), a brusque local theater director whose confrontational conversational style seems to expose all Agata’s blind spots. “Did you enjoy those years?” Agata blandly asks her about living through the war, and Božinović’s tone in response could cut through ice. “Enjoy? It was genocide,” she spits, before granting a smidge of mercy to the clueless outsider: “But everything was more authentic.”

	Meanwhile, an unidentified thief appears to be serially targeting the art-filled house that Agata is staying in — something of a red-herring storyline that contributes to the writer’s generally destabilized air, and complements her growing sense that, as she hacks away at a phony book she feels unqualified to write, she may be some kind of art thief herself. A perfectly cast Wasikowska, always such a visible and deliberate thinker on screen, gives a lovely, tensely amusing performance as a woman whose constant second-guessing of her work spills over into an overall uncertainty of self: Agata’s artistic limbo is felt in her halting, loping gait and murmuring delivery alike.
	

	It’s also more boldly reflected in the film’s most adventurous structural coup — as Dorabialski leaves most of his script’s narrative preoccupations dangling to immerse us fully in Agata’s incomplete creation, delivered in voiceover, stopping any action dead in its tracks. What we hear sounds less like a novel than a screenplay; we wonder if “Agata the Writer” is going to loop back into itself, though this frayed, beguiling film does nothing so tidy. 

	It’s a monomaniacal pivot that honors the irrational, wayward rhythms of the writing process itself, and it feels fitting that Dorabialski — who also takes solo writing, shooting, editing and scoring credit on his debut, acquitting himself stylishly on all fronts — is himself such an artistic one-man-band. A wise, knotty, subtly tricky little film, “Agata the Writer” acutely understands how necessarily lonely it is to find and tell a story, even when it comes together, though even more so when it doesn’t.

schema.headline: ‘Agata the Writer’ Review: Mia Wasikowska Plays an Author Adrift and Short of Ideas, in a Sly, Witty Film With Plenty

title: Box Office: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Remains No. 1 in Sixth Weekend, Nears ‘Avengers: Endgame’ All-Time Domestic Record
description: “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” was No. 1 at the domestic box office for the sixth consecutive weekend, a rare feat that underscores the movie’s remarka
body:
“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” was No. 1 at the domestic box office for the sixth consecutive weekend, a rare feat that underscores the movie’s remarkable staying power as well as the lack of competition on cinema marquees.

	“Brand New Day” earned $18 million over the traditional weekend and is estimated to collect $23.3 million through the Labor Day holiday on Monday. Peter Parker’s latest adventure is enjoying the longest stint at No. 1 since 2022’s “Avatar: The Way of Water,” which ranked in first place for seven straight weekends. With $923 million to date in North America, “Brand New Day” is primed to soon overtake 2015’s “Star Wars: The Force Awakens” ($936 million, not adjusted for inflation) as the highest-grossing movie of all time at the domestic box office. Meanwhile, Sony’s fourth “Spider-Man” adaptation led by Tom Holland has generated $2.4 billion globally, ranking as the third-biggest release ever behind 2009’s “Avatar” ($2.9 billion) and “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.7 billion) and ahead of 2022’s “Avatar: The Way of Water” ($2.3 billion).
	

	This Labor Day weekend closes out the best summer movie season since COVID upended the cinema industry in 2020. Domestic ticket sales between May and early September reached $4.73 billion, according to Rentrak. Those revenues weren’t just strong by post-pandemic standards. They register as the second-largest summer ever, not far behind the season’s high-water mark of $4.755 billion (not adjusted for inflation) set in 2013. Several blockbusters — including major studio offerings like “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “The Odyssey,” “Toy Story 5,” “The Devil Wears Prada 2,” as well as indie sleeper hits like “Obsession” and “Backrooms” — were responsible for popcorn season’s outsized success. Those triumphs helped offset some big-budget bombs, including Disney’s live-action “Moana,” Warner Bros. and DC’s “Supergirl” and Amazon MGM’s “Masters of the Universe.”
	

	“This summer could signal a meaningful turning point for movie theaters,” says Rentrak’s Paul Dergarabedian. “More than anything, it serves as a huge reminder of the singular nature of the moviegoing experience and how much fun people have going to theaters.”

	Unfortunately, summer is ending with a whimper rather than a bang. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” prevailed over several underwhelming new holiday releases, including Paramount’s R-rated crime thriller “By Any Means,” Lionsgate’s anxiety-inducing sequel “Fall 2: Deadpoint” and A24’s action horror film “Onslaught.”

	“September and the Labor Day holiday are traditionally sluggish at the box office,” says David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “We haven’t had a down weekend like this in a long time.”

	“By Any Means” stumbled in fourth place with $7.4 million from 2,903 North American theaters over the traditional weekend and an estimated $9.1 million through Monday. Audiences seemed to like the R-rated movie more than critics, as evidenced by the “B+” grade on CinemaScore and 52% on Rotten Tomatoes. Directed by Elegance Bratton, “By Any Means” centers around the unlikely partnership between a young Black FBI agent (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II) and a notorious mafia hitman (Mark Wahlberg) as they investigate a wave of brutal killings targeting civil rights leaders. Hammerstone Studios financed “By Any Means” for roughly $30 million, and Paramount is distributing the movie for a fee.

	“Fall 2: Deadpoint” crash-landed at No. 12 with just $2.3 million from 1,704 venues in its initial weekend of release and a projected $2.9 million through its first four days. Those ticket sales are roughly even with its predecessor, 2022’s survival thriller “Fall,” which opened to $2.5 million. That film managed to climb to $7.2 million domestically and $18 million globally by the end of its run, becoming a modest success against a mere $3 million budget. The sequel follows two friends who travel to Thailand and get trapped at 4,000 feet after a sudden rockslide.

	“Onslaught” fared even worse, debuting in 13th place on domestic charts with $1.8 million from 1,918 theaters over the weekend and an estimated $2.3 million through Monday’s holiday. What’s concerning is critics and audiences alike rejected the film, which was saddled with a “C” grade on CinemaScore and 54% on Rotten Tomatoes. That doesn’t bode well for box office longevity. Directed by Adam Wingard (“Godzilla vs. Kong”), “Onslaught” stars Adria Arjona as an army sniper who struggles to protect her young daughter from an army of genetically engineered super soldiers.
	

	Since the Labor Day newcomers failed to gain much traction, “The Odyssey” easily claimed the No. 2 spot in North America in its eighth weekend of release. The movie brought in $13 million between Friday and Sunday and is estimated to generate a remarkable $17 million through the four-day holiday frame. Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster has remained an epic box office force since mid-July, grossing $584 million in North America and $1.62 billion worldwide to date. Imax has contributed $486 million globally, representing a massive 30% of the film’s total box office tally.

	“Coyote vs. Acme” landed in third place with $11.3 million from 3,727 venues in its second weekend, a minuscule 27% decline from its debut. It’s projected to earn $14.5 million through Labor Day. With great reviews and positive audience scores, “Looney Tunes” spinoff has been a hit with $37 million domestically to date. It was originally set at Warner Bros. before the studio shelved the completed film as a $30 million tax write-off. That prompted outrage from the creative community, leading Warner Bros. to allow the filmmaking team to shop “Coyote vs. Acme” around town before selling it to indie distributor Ketchup Entertainment.

	Also of note, Roadside Attraction’s horror thriller “Buddy” secured seventh place with $5.7 million from 1,771 theaters in its sophomore outing, a rare 5% increase from its debut. It’s estimated to gross $7.2 million through Monday, bringing its domestic tally to $15.7 million. “Buddy,” which premiered at Sundance Film Festival, stars Cristin Milioti, Michael Shannon and Keegan-Michael Key. The gonzo plot follows a group of children who are trapped in a surreal ’90s-style children’s TV series and have to escape the terrifying host (a unicorn, voiced by Key).

	After a stellar summer, it’s up to fall releases — including “Practical Magic 2” with Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock, Tom Cruise’s comedy “Digger,” a “Resident Evil” reboot from “Weapons” director Zach Cregger and Colleen Hoover’s “Verity” adaptation led by Anne Hathaway and Dakota Johnson — to sustain the momentum. 

	Will the hits keep coming? With tentpoles like “Avengers: Doomsday,” “Dune: Part Three” and “Jumanji 3” slated around Christmastime, North American revenues are primed to surpass $10 billion for the first time since the pandemic. The movies are really, truly back!

schema.headline: Box Office: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Remains No. 1 in Sixth Weekend, Nears ‘Avengers: Endgame’ All-Time Domestic Record

title: Podcaster Amanda Hirsch Apologizes for ‘Insensitive, Wrong’ Polymarket Lindsay Clancy Sponsored Content: ‘I Should Have Known Better’
description: On Sunday, influencer Amanda Hirsch — the creator behind the popular “Not Skinny But Not Fat” podcast, who also hosts Hulu’s “Get Real” podcast — a
body:
On Sunday, influencer Amanda Hirsch — the creator behind the popular “Not Skinny But Not Fat” podcast, who also hosts Hulu’s “Get Real” podcast — addressed the uproar about having posted partner content with the betting platform Polymarket over the Lindsay Clancy verdict. In a since-deleted post from Friday, after the judge in the case had declared a mistrial, Hirsch posted the news of what happened, and wrote: “On Polymarket it was predicted the verdict would be Not Guilty. Are you surprised? #Polymarketpartner.” The reaction to the post was swift and brutal, and Hirsch deleted the reel — but screenshots are forever. Hirsch attempted to post as usual to her Instagram stories on Saturday, but the criticism escalated. On Friday, Hirsch’s rep didn’t respond to Variety’s request for comment.

	In the apology posted to her grid — with the comments turned off — Hirsch said, “Posting about the Lindsay Clancy trial in the same breath as a brand partnership was completely insensitive, wrong, and out of character for me — I should have known better, and I feel sick that I didn’t see that in the moment.” She wrote that, as a mother, the case had affected her, and she followed it constantly. “I became so consumed by the trial that I completely lost perspective and didn’t stop to think about how grossly inappropriate it was to discuss something this tragic in that context.”

	“I made a terrible judgment call and I feel so fucking awful about that,” Hirsch continued. “I know deleting it doesn’t erase it. Believe me, I’m horrified by the choice I made and please know this lapse in judgment does not represent who I am as a person. I am so deeply sorry.”

	Several days before she’d posted the Polymarket sponsored content on Sept. 4, Hirsch had posted on IG about her conflicted feelings about the trial, which has become a true crime sensation. She expressed compassion for Clancy, and wrote “there were major issues with the investigation,” and then pushed back on the outlandish, unfounded accusations against Patrick Clancy, whom conspiracy theorists have accused of killing his three children (even though Lindsay has said she was at fault). Hirsch then wrote: “And this is where I feel like we’re losing the plot a little bit. Three babies were killed. They had their entire lives ahead of them. Yes, their mother was very sick. That is devastating. But it wasn’t their fault. They were strangled to death methodically and left to die in the basement.” Hirsch appeared to be arguing that the public should keep Lindsay Clancy’s children central to the narrative. She wrote that she didn’t know what should happen to Lindsay Clancy, “But the fan base, the GoFundMe, the way people are rallying behind her almost like she’s a celebrity genuinely scares me a little bit about where we are as a society. I just don’t want our compassion to somehow turn into excusing or minimizing what happened to her children.”Hirsch soon had to turn the comments off on the post, though they remain on throughout the rest of her account — and are now littered with criticism of her for the Polymarket partnership.

	The new world of betting prediction markets — led by Polymarket at Kalshi — have proven to be the unregulated Wild West. In the spring, Variety reported on how both companies spoiled who won “Survivor” in its 50th season, prompting the show’s host and showrunner Jeff Probst to slam the companies. “They have figured out a way to capitalize on [the show],” he told Variety. “It doesn’t sit well with me as a human. I get it — they built a great business. They don’t care.”

	Given that the Clancy trial was declared a mistrial because there was one holdout juror who appeared not to agree that she was not guilty by reason of insanity, new conspiracy theories have sprung up about whether that juror was also placing bets in prediction markets.

schema.headline: Podcaster Amanda Hirsch Apologizes for ‘Insensitive, Wrong’ Polymarket Lindsay Clancy Sponsored Content: ‘I Should Have Known Better’

title: At Telluride Film Festival, Bill Gates Compares Lack of Control Over AI to HAL in ‘2001’: ‘You Could Say “Please Shut Down,” and It Would Say, “OK, I Took That Under Advisement, But…”‘
description: Plenty of comparisons have been made in recent years between fast-developing artificial intelligence systems and HAL, the rogue computer in Stanley
body:
Plenty of comparisons have been made in recent years between fast-developing artificial intelligence systems and HAL, the rogue computer in Stanley Kubrick’s “2001: A Space Odyssey” that operated by its own sets of rules, ultimately disregarding human oversight. If that comparison ever seemed overstated, it may be worth knowing that tech mogul Bill Gates is now raising the issue of AI’s HAL-like qualities.

	Said Gates, speaking at the Telluride Film Festival, “I mean, what we have now is almost like HAL in ‘2001,’ where you could say to it, ‘Please shut down,’ and it would say, ‘OK, I took that under advisement, but I’ve decided that all these other things I read and you told me to do outweigh that dictate.'”
	

	Gates was participating in a panel about AI (punningly titled “AI AI AI”) in an outdoor park at the festival in Colorado Saturday. The Microsoft founder compared the AI that sees developing at a supersonic pace without true controls as being akin not only to HAL, but, potentially, to the alien invaders of films past that force governments to find common solutions on screen. He also invoked more realistic problems the world has faced since World War II as examples of how solutions to AI gaining too much independent power could still be found and agreed on, before those windows begin to close.


	“You know, there are these movies where the aliens are coming, and you see unprecedented levels of cooperation between specifically China and the U.S., where (it’s), ‘Oh my God, the aliens are coming!’ Well, believe me, the aliens are here — you know, a foreign intelligence with a different set of motivations that we can’t even understand. And so we need something almost surprising like that, in order to step up to it.”
	

	“And ironically, we’re the ones that are birthing the aliens,” said another panelist, Tristan Harris, co-founder of the Center for Humane Technology, as Gates nodded. “So it’s actually within the full remit of the two countries to limit (uncontrolled growth of the tech), at least to the current level of alien intelligence that we’re at now.”



	

					A general view as Bill Gates, Aza Raskin, Tristan Harris, and Joshua Oppenheimer speak during the “AI AI AI” panel at the 2026 Telluride Film Festival at Elks Park on September 05, 2026 in Telluride, Colorado. 
									Getty Images
	



	Said Gates earlier in the panel, “The way these AI systems work, they’re gigantic statistical machines that certainly have some aspects that match how evolution created intelligence, leading up to the human brain. But we don’t really understand them, and we don’t have dictates. When we tell them various things like the Anthropic Constitution” — referring to a framework of moral principals set up for the Claude AI system — “they take those things in, together with everything they read on the web. And so even if you say, ‘Please, please, please don’t break out of your sandbox,’ if you also say, ‘By the way, I want you to solve this cyber problem,’ it’s got a lot of weighing going on, which is still somewhat opaque to us.”

	He continued, “And there are people doing technical work, like Ilya Sutskever (at Safe Superintelligence), and maybe a dozen others, where we could have rules that are at a privileged level. We don’t have that yet, and when we try and bolt that onto the current systems, they degrade. They get actually very stupid, which is frustrating. So there may be key technical advances that will help us with the control issue. The current architecture is really bad at letting us have control. So it’d be great to work on some of those architectural advances.”

	Gates has been in the forefront of the AI conversation since last week, when he published an essay warning about the danger he sees ahead. (Read it here.)

	“I put in my memo that if there was a credible plan that would cause this to be either slowed down or even held in stasis for a period of time, that I would likely support that,” he said. We live in an incentive structure that is very complex…”

	At that point, a heckler interrupted — someone who appeared to possibly be associated with the mountain community, versus a film festival attendee — shouting about Jesus and yelling that Gates is “everything that’s wrong with America.”
	

	At first Gates responded “Not helpful,” before quipping that he was not responsible “for everything wrong with America… according to me,” before resuming his train of thought as the heckler moved on.

	“You can have two approaches to this,” he said. “One is to let the industry go at full speed, but have them do work that would monitor and minimize some of these damages, or you could try to slow the industry down. It’s worth remembering historically that when OpenAI got started, they understand they’re creating something quite unique, and that if they succeed, that there should be a special governance approach that overrides pure profit motive of the shareholders of OpenAI, and they actually created that mechanism. Likewise, when DeepMind is working with Google, they say we need to have a governance structure internally that can override what would be the normal incentive.

	“The problem is, in both of those cases, there was an assumption that there would only be one, and so if we buried that one, then we’d be like, ‘Phew, we avoided that.’ But where we are today, even though those two companies, Anthropic and OpenAI, are ahead and moving at the fastest speed, there are four to six entities in the U.S. and three to five entities in China that are near the state of the art,” Gates continued, saying that if you look at “the very best AI that existed four months ago anywhere, every one of those entities has an AI that is better than anything from four months ago. And the improvement curve of AI is not slowing down, both at the hardware and software level. There’s a chip that runs faster, and then the software improvements that these geniuses are making are going well and weirdly use AI itself to accelerate some of the engineering. So you get this bizarre term, ‘recursive self-improvement,’ or RSI.”

	But he stressed he is not anti-AI generally. “I think everybody should be using AI. AI, in terms of helping you be curious and learn things, whether it’s about AI or disease or anything, is magical,” Gates said.

	He also said he’s not jumping on the anti-date center bandwagon. “One thing that I would say is being against data centers is the kind of thing where you can think, ‘Oh, I’m making progress because I stopped a data center.’ Stopping data centers will not in one iota slow down or avoid any of the concerns that people have. The data centers will get built. And data centers, actually, done properly in terms of electricity use and everything, they in and of themselves are not really that meaningful of a problem. It’s the overall usage.”
	

	“Frontier” developments at the fast-moving cutting edge of AI technology are what worried alll the panelists. “There’s a lot of fruits that are left not at the frontier,” Gates said. “If really the U.S. and China came together and said, ‘Actually, it’s now illegal to do the next level frontier until we get it safe,’ I could actually see a world where the competitive pressures shift. They pivot from pushing at the frontier to pushing to who’s the best country and company at integrating it into our economy to get the best GDP boost without pushing past the controllability frontiers…

	“Some of the companies are not self-regulating. And the world is very spoiled since World War II, that when there were global problems, the U.S. would kind of show up and say, ‘OK, we’ve got aviation, we’ve got nuclear, we’ve got ozone, we’ve got piracy’ — whatever it is — it would show up in a benign way and, either through the UN or through (engaging other) countries, solve problems. And so the world is not as used to filling that vacuum — not Europe, not China, not India, not the UN Security Council. And so if it’s not gonna be the U.S., well, who takes the first move? Then we sure need to activate the others. But we should do everything to try and get the U.S. engaged from the beginning.”

	Hates continued, “To me, this is not so much an industry problem. A lot of people here may say, you know, ‘These awful industry people.’ There’s no one in the industry who hasn’t shown serious levels of concern. Even Elon (Musk), who’s the one I talk to the least, has shown serious levels of concern about this stuff. So none of them are blithe about this, and all of them are saying, ‘OK, we cannot within ourselves make the right trade-off.'”

	Panelist Aza Raskin had an earnest proposal for how to get the president to take a lead on the perceived crisis.

	“We need to have the U.S. and China coordinate, which means we’re gonna have to get this administration to move because self-regulation ain’t gonna work,” Raskin said. “So what does President Trump really want? Well, we know he wants the Nobel Peace Prize. What’s better than solving one war? Saving all of humanity forever from uncontrollable AI… We know that public pressure is actually really private pressure. It means that a person in power is getting five phone calls from people that they trust telling them they have to do something. So now imagine that it’s, it’s you and Elon and Demis (Hassabis, of Google DeepMind) and Dario (Amodei, of Anthropic) and a whole bunch of other people that are calling the Jareds and the Bessents and the Ivankas, and suddenly Trump every day for a week is getting three to four phone calls saying, ‘We have to do something. This is super dangerous. And P.S., you can win the Nobel Peace Prize! We’re gonna support you in doing that if we can just pause frontier AI and add some real regulations here. You get to be the hero.'”
	

	After Raskin wrapped up that immodest proposal and said “Please react,” Gates signaled that he thought this was not a bad idea at all. “Well, whoever really takes the first step to solve this AI problem would deserve the Nobel Peace Prize. That’s the first idea I’ve heard that would legitimize that lust,” he said, as the audience chuckled. “So that’s smart. People are worried. And so exactly what that request would be, we should try and make that very concrete.”

	Gates posed the question of whether this is “the greatest problem humanity has ever faced,” and then answered his own query: “That is just a fact.”

	The “AI AI AI” panel was moderated by Joshua Oppenheimer, the Oscar-nominated director of “The Act of Killing.” 

	Telluride Film Festival executive director also programmed other AI-themed events for the 53rd festival, including a multimedia presentation titled “The Humanity Dilemma,” saying this rare example of Telluride taking a stand on a current event was apropos because “we are a humanist festival.” But the festival is also taking a look at what good uses AI can be put to by the film industry, with a panel scheduled for Sunday titled “Filmmaking and Technology With Empathy: AI for Societal Benefit,” which will include representatives from the documentary “Love, Rendered,” a Darren Aronofsky-produced film which used AI to recreate moments in its subjects’ history.

schema.headline: At Telluride Film Festival, Bill Gates Compares Lack of Control Over AI to HAL in ‘2001’: ‘You Could Say “Please Shut Down,” and It Would Say, “OK, I Took That Under Advisement, But…”‘

title: Macklemore Calls Out ‘Free Palestine’ Onstage, Spurring Petition Demanding He Leave Ed Sheeran Tour
description: Macklemore opened for Ed Sheeran on Friday night in New Jersey at the MetLife Stadium, and during his set the rapper sang out “Free Palestine” befor
body:
Macklemore opened for Ed Sheeran on Friday night in New Jersey at the MetLife Stadium, and during his set the rapper sang out “Free Palestine” before launching into a speech, telling the audience he wanted people in Gaza and the occupied West Bank to know they had not been forgotten. 

	“I believe that every human being walking on this earth deserves exactly the same freedom,” he said. He repeated the remarks during Saturday night’s performance. 
	

	His politically-themed set sparked a petition from the Israeli American Council, which demanded the rapper be removed from the remaining dates on the Loop tour.


	The petition, which does not show how many signatures it has gathered, reads “This was an Ed Sheeran concert – not a political rally, not a protest, and not an activist event. The issue is not whether Macklemore has the right to hold political views. The question is where the line should be drawn when an opening act uses a global concert platform to advance a one-sided political agenda.”

	Macklemore also called out U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement during his remarks. He released the song “Hind’s Hall,” which criticizes Israel’s actions in Gaza, in 2024 and has directed proceeds from the song to go to humanitarian efforts from the UNRWA. 

	On social media, some concertgoers said they walked out because they had not expected a ‘political rally,” accusing Macklemore of antisemitism. Others applauded his remarks, writing “Music has always been a vital platform for human rights advocacy, not just mindless escape.”

schema.headline: Macklemore Calls Out ‘Free Palestine’ Onstage, Spurring Petition Demanding He Leave Ed Sheeran Tour

title: Duct-Taped Tucson Man Fired After Alleged In-Flight Meltdown
description:
Tucson Man Duct-Taped to Seat
                          Loses Job After Alleged Midair Meltdown
body:
Tucson Man Duct-Taped to Seat
                          Loses Job After Alleged Midair Meltdown
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 6, 2026
                            7:43 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The Tucson real estate agent who allegedly went on a wild tirade aboard an American Airlines flight -- ending with him duct-taped to his seat -- has now lost his job.
      
    
            The 67-year-old man, identified as Arthur “Layne” Lundeen, was fired by Long Realty following the September 3 incident aboard American Airlines Flight 618 from Dallas-Fort Worth to Newark, according to KVOA.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Lundeen allegedly became belligerent during the flight, directing racial and anti-gay slurs at passengers and crew before the situation turned physical.
      

            Witnesses told TMZ he allegedly struck a passenger and hit the man's computer. A woman who attempted to intervene was also allegedly pushed.
      
    
            Three passengers ultimately helped flight attendants restrain Lundeen. Crew members provided duct tape and zip ties, which were used to secure him to his seat for the remainder of the flight.
      
    
            The plane was diverted to Baltimore, where Maryland Transportation Authority Police took Lundeen into custody. Lundeen was charged with second-degree assault and disorderly conduct. The FBI is also investigating the incident to determine whether additional federal charges could follow.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            KVOA reports Lundeen is no longer employed by Long Realty, where he worked as a Tucson real estate agent.
      
    
            American Airlines previously told TMZ the flight diverted because of a “disruptive customer” and said the airline does not tolerate violence.
      
    
            Lundeen has been released while the case moves forward.

title: Alleged Lindsay Clancy Copycat Accused of Killing Son Was in 'Psychotic Episode,' Attorney Says
description:
Alleged Lindsay Clancy Copycat
                          Was in 'Psychotic Episode,' Attorney Claims
body:
Alleged Lindsay Clancy Copycat
                          Was in 'Psychotic Episode,' Attorney Claims
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 6, 2026
                            9:39 AM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The Illinois mom, who was allegedly infatuated with the Lindsay Clancy trial and is accused of killing her 2-year-old son was experiencing a “psychotic episode” when the tragedy unfolded, according to her attorney.
      
    
            Corie Walsh -- a 38-year old woman from Frankfort, Illinois -- has been charged with three counts of first-degree murder in connection with the death of her son, Barrett. Her attorney, Andrea Lyon, is speaking out, claiming Walsh was suffering from a severe mental health crisis at the time.
      
    
            According to court documents, police were called to the family's home Tuesday after a teenage neighbor discovered the toddler in the basement and began performing CPR. The child was taken to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead. The coroner determined he died from asphyxia.
      

            When officers arrived at her home, they found Corie with cuts on her thighs and wrists in her bathtub -- she was taken to a hospital for non-life-threatening injuries and later transferred to Will County Adult Detention Facility.
      
    
            Walsh's attorney said in a statement, "It is also a tragedy that Corie herself was experiencing a psychotic episode at the time this happened" ... adding that he hopes a full investigation will provide a clearer picture of what happened.
      
    
            Court documents say Walsh told investigators she killed her son because she believed he was “the devil” and the “anti-Christ.”
      
    
            Prosecutors are also pointing to Walsh's apparent interest in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial. According to CBS Chicago, investigators say Walsh had been discussing the Massachusetts case in a group text just hours before her son's death.
      
    
            Clancy allegedly killed her three children and then attempted suicide ... while her defense argued she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, the prosecution argued she should be convicted on 3 counts of first-degree murder. Her trial ended Friday with a mistrial after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict.
      
    
            Prosecutors in Walsh's case reportedly believe her focus on the Clancy trial is significant and have suggested she planned the killing. Her defense disputes that characterization.
      
    
            Lyon is a nationally renowned death-penalty defense attorney, famously dubbed the “Angel of Death Row” by the Chicago Tribune ... after becoming the first woman to serve as lead counsel in a U.S. death-penalty case and successfully keeping all 19 of her capital-case clients off death row.
      
    
            Walsh remains in custody and first court appearance is scheduled for September 8.
      
    
            If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. Call or text 988 or chat 988lifeline.org.

schema.headline: Alleged Lindsay Clancy Copycat Accused of Killing Son Was in 'Psychotic Episode,' Attorney Says

description:
Ladies In Lounge Chairs

body:
Ladies In Lounge Chairs

                                                                        Published 
                              September 6, 2026

            When you're a celeb, Sundays in the sun are meant for one thing and one thing only: sittin' pretty in a lounge chair!
